title: GERD: Diagnose the Syndrome, Identify Alarm Features, Use the Lowest Effective Long-Term Strategy
bottomLine: Typical reflux without alarm features is often diagnosed clinically and managed with lifestyle/acid suppression as appropriate. Dysphagia, GI bleeding/anemia, weight loss, persistent vomiting or refractory symptoms change the pathway toward endoscopic/diagnostic evaluation; long-term PPI use should have a continuing indication rather than automatic indefinite renewal.
recognize: Heartburn/regurgitation related to meals/position supports GERD; cough, throat symptoms and chest pain have broader differentials and should not be attributed to reflux reflexively.
GERD can coexist with obesity, hiatal hernia, pregnancy and selected medications.
differentiate: Cardiac ischemia must be considered in compatible chest pain before attributing symptoms to reflux.
Eosinophilic esophagitis, peptic stricture, malignancy and motility disease can present with dysphagia and require diagnostic evaluation.
assessment: Assess symptom pattern, dysphagia/odynophagia, bleeding/anemia, weight loss, vomiting, medication triggers, pregnancy, NSAIDs and prior endoscopy.
Clarify whether symptoms recur off therapy and whether the PPI is being taken correctly.
workup: Use empiric therapy for uncomplicated typical symptoms when appropriate; use endoscopy for alarm features or refractory/complicated disease.
Use pH testing/motility studies selectively when diagnosis remains uncertain before invasive/long-term decisions.
management: Use weight/meal/timing strategies when relevant and PPI/H2RA therapy matched to severity.
Step to the lowest effective maintenance strategy when symptoms/complications allow, while continuing necessary therapy for high-risk indications.
medicationSafety: Review whether chronic PPI therapy still has a valid indication rather than stopping or continuing automatically.
Avoid abrupt interpretation of nonspecific symptoms as PPI adverse effects without assessing the underlying indication and alternatives.
counselling: Teach timing/adherence and which alarm symptoms require reassessment rather than repeated OTC self-treatment.
followUp: Reassess response/ongoing indication and close the loop on endoscopy/pathology if alarm features develop.
examTrap: Calling dysphagia 'reflux' and escalating the PPI without investigating obstruction/eosinophilic disease/malignancy.
oneLinePearl: Uncomplicated GERD can be clinical; alarm features make it diagnostic.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology GERD/upper-GI practice resources

title: Peptic Ulcer Disease and H. pylori: Find the Cause, Eradicate Correctly, Prove Cure When Indicated
bottomLine: Peptic ulcer disease is usually driven by H. pylori, NSAID/antiplatelet exposure or less common hypersecretory/malignant causes. Test for H. pylori with an appropriate active-infection test, use a current eradication regimen informed by resistance/previous antibiotic exposure, and confirm eradication rather than assuming symptom improvement means cure.
recognize: Epigastric pain, GI bleeding, iron-deficiency anemia or occult bleeding can occur; ulcer complications include hemorrhage, perforation and gastric-outlet obstruction.
NSAIDs, aspirin and H. pylori can have additive ulcer risk.
differentiate: Dyspepsia is a symptom syndrome and does not prove an ulcer.
Serology may remain positive after prior infection and is not the preferred test to prove active infection or cure.
assessment: Assess bleeding, weight loss, vomiting, NSAIDs/aspirin/anticoagulants, prior H. pylori treatment/antibiotics, smoking and family/cancer risk.
workup: Use urea-breath or stool-antigen testing for active infection when appropriate and account for PPI/antibiotic/bismuth effects on test accuracy.
Use endoscopy for alarm features, significant bleeding or other guideline-supported indications.
management: Use a current Canadian/local H. pylori eradication regimen selected to prior macrolide/metronidazole exposure, allergies and resistance context rather than memorizing an obsolete universal triple therapy.
Stop/reduce ulcerogenic NSAID exposure when possible and provide appropriate gastroprotection when it must continue.
Confirm eradication after treatment using an appropriate active-infection test.
medicationSafety: Check antibiotic interactions/allergies and pregnancy context.
PPI use around eradication testing can cause false-negative results and requires protocol-appropriate holding.
counselling: Explain that feeling better does not prove H. pylori eradication and that completing the full regimen matters.
followUp: Confirm cure and reassess persistent symptoms/ulcer healing where the clinical indication requires it.
examTrap: Repeating an outdated clarithromycin-based regimen without reviewing prior macrolide exposure/resistance—or skipping test-of-cure because symptoms improved.
oneLinePearl: H. pylori care has two endpoints: finish effective therapy and prove eradication.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology H. pylori practice guidance

title: Dyspepsia: Alarm Features, H. pylori, and a Structured Trial Before Endoscopy
bottomLine: Dyspepsia is upper-abdominal discomfort/early satiety/postprandial fullness, not a diagnosis of ulcer or reflux. Screen for alarm/cancer risk, use H. pylori test-and-treat and/or an appropriate acid-suppression trial in low-risk patients, and reserve endoscopy for age/risk/alarm or refractory patterns where it will change care.
recognize: Epigastric pain/burning, early satiety and postprandial fullness are typical; nausea/bloating can coexist.
Functional dyspepsia is diagnosed after appropriate evaluation rather than assumed at the first visit.
differentiate: Cardiac, biliary, pancreatic and medication causes can mimic upper-GI symptoms.
New dysphagia, bleeding/anemia, weight loss or persistent vomiting require a different pathway from uncomplicated dyspepsia.
assessment: Assess age/risk, alarm symptoms, NSAID use, H. pylori history, reflux, biliary/pancreatic features, pregnancy and medication triggers.
workup: Use noninvasive H. pylori testing and targeted labs where appropriate; use endoscopy based on alarm/risk/refractory criteria rather than routinely for every patient.
management: Use H. pylori eradication when positive and a defined PPI trial when appropriate.
For persistent functional dyspepsia, use diet/trigger review and evidence-based neuromodulator/prokinetic/psychological strategies selectively rather than endless acid escalation.
medicationSafety: Avoid chronic NSAID exposure when it plausibly contributes.
Do not continue multiple empiric GI medications indefinitely without reassessing the diagnosis.
counselling: Explain the stepwise plan and when symptom evolution should trigger endoscopy or another differential.
followUp: Review response to each defined trial and investigate persistent/alarm disease rather than stacking treatments.
examTrap: Ordering immediate endoscopy for every low-risk young patient with uncomplicated dyspepsia—or calling new dysphagia functional dyspepsia.
oneLinePearl: Dyspepsia management is risk-stratified: alarms first, H. pylori/defined trial next, endoscopy when it adds value.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology dyspepsia guidance

title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Confirm Inflammation, Define Extent, Treat to Control Disease and Complications
bottomLine: IBD diagnosis requires objective intestinal inflammation and phenotype/extent assessment; IBS symptoms alone are not IBD. Management is severity/phenotype driven with steroid-sparing maintenance, infection/vaccine safety and dysplasia surveillance coordinated with gastroenterology.
recognize: Chronic diarrhea, blood, urgency, abdominal pain, weight loss, anemia and extraintestinal joint/skin/eye disease support IBD.
Crohn disease can be transmural and affect any GI segment; ulcerative colitis is continuous colonic mucosal disease beginning at the rectum.
differentiate: Infectious colitis, ischemia, celiac disease and IBS can mimic parts of IBD.
A normal CRP does not exclude active intestinal inflammation in every patient; stool inflammatory markers and endoscopy are context dependent.
assessment: Assess stool frequency/blood, nocturnal symptoms, weight/nutrition, fever, perianal disease, extraintestinal symptoms, smoking, NSAIDs, pregnancy and prior infections/biologic exposure.
workup: Use CBC/iron/inflammation, stool infection testing and fecal calprotectin when useful, then endoscopy/biopsy and imaging to confirm/type/extent disease.
Before biologic/targeted immune therapy, complete infection and vaccination screening appropriate to the drug.
management: Use 5-ASA, corticosteroids, immunomodulators/biologics/small molecules according to UC/Crohn phenotype and severity; corticosteroids induce control but are not maintenance therapy.
Escalate toxic colitis, obstruction, abscess, perforation or severe bleeding urgently and coordinate surgery when required.
medicationSafety: Immunosuppressive therapies have infection, malignancy and laboratory monitoring requirements; drug choice changes with pregnancy and prior infection.
Avoid chronic NSAIDs when they worsen disease and avoid repeated steroid dependence.
counselling: Teach medication adherence, vaccination/infection precautions, smoking cessation in Crohn disease and when severe symptoms require urgent care.
followUp: Track objective disease control as well as symptoms and maintain colon-cancer/dysplasia surveillance through the specialist pathway.
examTrap: Maintaining IBD long term with repeated prednisone bursts without a steroid-sparing disease-control plan.
oneLinePearl: IBD treatment aims for durable inflammatory control, not repeated rescue steroids.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology IBD clinical practice guidance

title: IBS: Make a Positive Diagnosis After Checking the Red Flags
bottomLine: IBS is a disorder of gut–brain interaction that can be diagnosed positively from a compatible symptom pattern after limited targeted testing and absence of alarm features; it does not require exhaustive exclusion of every GI disease, but blood loss, weight loss, nocturnal/progressive symptoms or inflammatory clues require another pathway.
recognize: Recurrent abdominal pain related to defecation and change in stool frequency/form supports IBS; constipation-, diarrhea- and mixed-predominant patterns guide therapy.
Symptoms can fluctuate with diet, stress, sleep and other gut-brain factors without being 'all psychological'.
differentiate: Celiac disease, IBD, colorectal cancer, infection, medication effects and thyroid/metabolic disease can mimic IBS when the phenotype/risk fits.
Rectal bleeding and iron-deficiency anemia are not explained by IBS.
assessment: Assess pain/stool pattern, duration, weight, bleeding, nocturnal symptoms, family history, medication/diet and psychosocial impact.
Use non-stigmatizing language and screen for eating-disorder risk before restrictive diets.
workup: Use limited CBC/celiac/inflammatory or stool testing based on subtype and risk; avoid repetitive imaging/endoscopy when a stable typical pattern has already been appropriately evaluated.
management: Use subtype-based soluble fibre, selected low-FODMAP/dietitian support, antispasmodic/laxative/antidiarrheal/secretagogue or neuromodulator therapy as appropriate.
Treat pelvic-floor dysfunction and psychological/gut-directed therapy when relevant without implying symptoms are imagined.
medicationSafety: Avoid chronic opioids for IBS pain because they can worsen bowel dysfunction and dependence.
Restrictive diets should be time-limited/structured to avoid nutritional harm.
counselling: Explain IBS as altered gut sensitivity/motility/brain-gut processing and set functional goals rather than promising cure from one food elimination.
followUp: Reassess subtype, function and evolving alarm features; stop ineffective therapies rather than accumulating them.
examTrap: Ordering repeated colonoscopies for stable IBS without new alarm features—or calling iron-deficiency anemia part of IBS.
oneLinePearl: IBS is a positive pattern diagnosis, but alarm features always reopen the differential.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology IBS guidance

title: Celiac Disease: Test While the Patient Is Eating Gluten, Then Treat Nutritional and Autoimmune Consequences
bottomLine: Celiac disease is immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by gluten. Test before the patient starts a gluten-free diet whenever possible, using appropriate IgA-based serology plus total IgA and confirmatory pathways; management requires a strict gluten-free diet with dietitian support and correction/monitoring of nutritional/bone/associated autoimmune complications.
recognize: Diarrhea, bloating, iron deficiency, weight loss, osteopenia, dermatitis herpetiformis or unexplained transaminase elevation can occur; many patients lack classic diarrhea.
Type 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroid disease and first-degree family history raise risk.
differentiate: Non-celiac gluten/wheat sensitivity and wheat allergy are distinct diagnoses.
Starting a gluten-free diet before testing can normalize serology/histology and make diagnosis difficult.
assessment: Assess GI symptoms, anemia/nutrient deficiency, weight/growth, fractures, autoimmune disease, family history and current gluten intake.
workup: Use tissue-transglutaminase IgA plus total IgA in the usual pathway; use IgG-based testing when IgA deficient and gastroenterology/biopsy confirmation according to age/context.
Assess iron/folate/B12/vitamin D/bone and other consequences when clinically indicated.
management: Use a lifelong strict gluten-free diet with experienced dietitian support and address nutrient deficiencies.
Evaluate persistent symptoms for accidental gluten exposure, refractory disease or another diagnosis rather than prescribing empiric immunosuppression.
medicationSafety: Avoid unnecessary supplements beyond demonstrated risk/deficiency and check medication excipients if clinically relevant.
counselling: Teach label/cross-contamination issues and emphasize that diagnostic testing is most reliable before gluten avoidance.
followUp: Track symptoms, serology/adherence and nutritional/bone consequences; reassess persistent abnormalities.
examTrap: Telling the patient to try gluten-free eating before celiac serology/biopsy evaluation and then trying to diagnose celiac after tests normalize.
oneLinePearl: Test first while gluten is still in the diet; treat with a supported lifelong gluten-free plan after diagnosis.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology/celiac clinical practice

title: Hepatitis B and C: Define Active Infection, Fibrosis, Coinfection, and Treatment Linkage
bottomLine: HBV and HCV testing must distinguish exposure from active infection, then define liver disease/fibrosis and transmission/pregnancy/coinfection context. HCV RNA confirms active HCV and most patients should be linked to curative direct-acting antiviral treatment; HBV treatment/monitoring is phase- and risk-based under the 2025 Canadian HBV guidance.
recognize: Chronic viral hepatitis can be asymptomatic despite progressive fibrosis/cirrhosis.
Pregnancy, HIV/HDV coinfection, immune suppression and cirrhosis change urgency/management.
differentiate: HCV antibody shows exposure and can remain positive after cure; HCV RNA identifies current viremia.
HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBs, HBeAg/anti-HBe and HBV DNA answer different questions; one positive HBV marker does not define treatment need.
assessment: Assess birth/travel/endemic-region risk, injection/sexual/household exposure, prior treatment, alcohol, pregnancy, medications and signs of advanced liver disease.
Use stigma-free counselling and assess vaccination/household-contact needs for HBV.
workup: Confirm active HCV with RNA and stage fibrosis/liver function; use HBV serology plus HBV DNA/ALT and fibrosis assessment according to the 2025 CASL/AMMI framework.
Screen relevant coinfections and HCC surveillance indications.
management: Link active HCV to direct-acting antiviral therapy through current Canadian treatment pathways.
Use current CASL/AMMI HBV treatment algorithms based on viral activity, liver disease and risk rather than treating every chronic HBsAg-positive patient identically.
Vaccinate susceptible contacts/patients for HBV as appropriate.
medicationSafety: DAAs have important interactions and renal/hepatic considerations; verify the regimen.
HBV reactivation can occur with immunosuppression and requires screening/prophylaxis/monitoring according to treatment risk.
counselling: Explain that HCV antibody can stay positive after cure and that HBV often requires long-term monitoring even when treatment is not currently indicated.
followUp: Confirm HCV treatment response and maintain fibrosis/HCC follow-up where indicated; monitor HBV phase/treatment/HCC risk longitudinally.
examTrap: Calling a positive HCV antibody active infection without RNA or treating all chronic HBV the same without DNA/ALT/fibrosis context.
oneLinePearl: HCV RNA answers 'active now'; HBV needs phase, viral load and liver-risk context.

title: MASLD: Stage Fibrosis Risk, Treat Metabolic Disease, Refer High-Risk Liver Disease
bottomLine: The generator slug uses legacy NAFLD wording, but current learner-facing terminology is metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). The key primary-care task is not detecting steatosis alone—it is identifying fibrosis risk, excluding competing causes and aggressively managing cardiometabolic disease.
recognize: MASLD is common with type 2 diabetes, central adiposity, dyslipidemia and hypertension and may occur with normal or mildly elevated aminotransferases.
Advanced fibrosis can exist despite modest enzyme abnormalities.
differentiate: Steatosis can result from alcohol, medications, viral hepatitis and other causes; document alcohol exposure and competing liver disease rather than assuming MASLD from imaging alone.
MASH indicates steatohepatitis/injury but fibrosis stage is the major prognostic liver variable.
assessment: Assess diabetes, BP, lipids, adiposity, OSA, alcohol, medications and signs of advanced liver disease.
Use non-stigmatizing chronic-disease language and avoid attributing disease to willpower.
workup: Use noninvasive fibrosis assessment such as FIB-4 and second-line elastography/specialty tools according to age/risk and local pathway.
Exclude viral/autoimmune/other liver disease when pattern or risk requires it.
management: Treat diabetes, obesity, lipids, BP and cardiovascular risk aggressively; use evidence-based obesity/diabetes pharmacotherapy when otherwise indicated.
Refer high/indeterminate fibrosis risk, cirrhosis, diagnostic uncertainty or decompensation to hepatology.
medicationSafety: Statins are not routinely contraindicated simply because MASLD is present and are important when vascular risk indicates them.
Avoid unproven supplements marketed as liver detoxification.
counselling: Focus on metabolic/liver/cardiovascular outcomes rather than weight blame; explain why fibrosis risk matters more than the word 'fatty'.
followUp: Reassess fibrosis/metabolic risk at an interval appropriate to risk and maintain cirrhosis/HCC care when indicated.
examTrap: Reassuring a patient because ALT is near normal despite high fibrosis risk—or stopping a needed statin just because steatosis is present.
oneLinePearl: In MASLD, find fibrosis risk and treat the metabolic/cardiovascular disease—not the ultrasound word alone.
sourceBasis: Obesity Canada 2025 pharmacotherapy update where metabolic treatment is indicated

title: Alcohol-Associated Liver Disease: Diagnose the Liver Syndrome and Treat Alcohol Use Without Stigma
bottomLine: The generator uses legacy 'alcoholic liver disease' wording; learner-facing care uses alcohol-associated liver disease. Quantify alcohol exposure nonjudgmentally, identify steatosis/hepatitis/fibrosis/cirrhosis and competing causes, assess withdrawal/nutrition/infection severity, and treat alcohol use disorder as a core component of liver treatment rather than moralizing or waiting for abstinence before offering care.
recognize: Alcohol-associated disease ranges from steatosis to inflammatory hepatitis and cirrhosis; aminotransferase pattern alone does not stage severity.
Jaundice, fever, malnutrition and coagulopathy in a heavy-drinking patient can indicate severe alcohol-associated hepatitis but infection and other liver causes must be evaluated.
differentiate: MASLD, viral hepatitis, drug injury and autoimmune disease can coexist; alcohol history does not exclude another diagnosis.
Withdrawal risk is a separate acute safety problem from liver severity.
assessment: Use validated alcohol screening and quantify pattern/last use, withdrawal history, nutrition, medications, social supports and other substance use.
Assess jaundice, encephalopathy, ascites, GI bleeding, infection, renal injury and withdrawal signs.
workup: Use CBC, liver/synthetic/renal/electrolyte tests and ultrasound/fibrosis assessment according to the syndrome; investigate infection and competing liver causes when appropriate.
Use severity scores only when they will inform specialist/hospital management—not as stand-alone diagnosis.
management: Treat decompensation/withdrawal/nutrition deficiencies and infection promptly and coordinate hepatology for severe hepatitis/cirrhosis.
Offer evidence-based AUD treatment and psychosocial/addiction support, including pharmacotherapy when liver status and contraindications permit.
Transplant/hepatology referral should not be delayed by stigmatizing assumptions; follow program-specific assessment.
medicationSafety: AUD medication selection changes with liver/renal disease and opioid exposure.
Avoid NSAIDs and unnecessary sedatives in decompensated cirrhosis where bleeding/renal/encephalopathy risk is high.
counselling: Use person-first language, discuss safer change/abstinence goals and connect patients with addiction treatment without requiring shame or punishment.
followUp: Track liver recovery/fibrosis/decompensation and AUD treatment; maintain HCC/variceal care when cirrhosis is present.
examTrap: Attributing every abnormal liver test to alcohol and missing viral/medication disease—or refusing liver/addiction treatment until the patient proves abstinence.
oneLinePearl: Alcohol-associated liver care treats two diseases together: liver injury and alcohol use disorder.
sourceBasis: Canadian hepatology alcohol-associated liver disease practice
